Rt. Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 240, to amend the Public Archives Act. He said:	This Bill proposes a very slight
amendment to chapter 4 of the statutes of 1912. It provides that:
Unless otherwise ordered by the Governor in Council, the powers and duties of the minister under this Act shall not be exercised or discharged by deputy except so far as the Dominion Archivist is authorized to act for or as the deputy of the minister.
It has been suggested that the archives should 'be created into a separate department, inasmuch as there is some difficulty in carrying on the business of the archives owing to the fact that its location is altogether separate from the Department of the Secretary of State, who is the minister of the department. This does not seem necessary; but at the same time it should be placed in such a position that the Archivist can, with the assistance of an accountant or other suitable officer, carry on the business of the archives with a much less

amount of red tape as to very small transactions than has been necessary in the past.
Will Dr. Doughty become a deputy minister under this Bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He was accorded the rank and status of a deputy minister last year; but, as the archives was not created into a department, it has been necessary, every time the officers have required a small amount of stationery, a bottle of ink, or any trifling article of that kind, to make a requisition and get in touch with the Department of the Secretary of State. If they have desired to send out $50 or $100 to any of the men who are constantly employed in doing work for the archives in various parts of the country, there has been a good deal of delay and inconvenience. I am quite convinced that the arrangement now proposed will he attended with considerable advantage in the administration of all matters connected with the archives.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE MR. JAMES P. BROWN.
speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I think it only fitting that reference should be made to the untimely decease of one of our colleagues, who has been a member of this House for more than twenty-two years. I refer to Mr. Brown, the late member for Chateauguay. I am sure that all of us, irrespective of party, will join in conveying to the family and friends of the deceased our deep sympathy and our appreciation of his worth as a member of this House. It was not my privilege to know Mr. Brown very intimately, but I do know that he was highly respected on 'both sides of the House; that he was a man who gave very devoted and constant attention to his duties as a .member; and I am sure that his death is a loss not only to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, whose colleague more especially he was, but to the House as a whole. On 'behalf of the members on this side of the House, I beg to tender to hon. gentlemen on the other side as well as to the family and friends of the deceased, our very deep and appreciative sympathy on this occasion.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. JAMES P. BROWN.
speechtext:
I am grateful to my right hon. friend for the very kind words he has just spoken regarding the decease of our lamented friend and colleague, Mr. Brown. As my right ,hon. friend has stated, Mr. Brown was a highly respected member of this House. Although he did not take a very great part in our discussions, it was my privilege to know him for many years and to appreciate the soundness of his judgment, the integrity of his character, the firmness of his disposition, and the cordiality of his relations with his
friends and neighbours. He represented the county of Chateauguay, which contains a mixed population of Scottish and French descent, and he represented it to the satisfaction of all races. He was a man of broad sympathies, who could reach all races and creeds without giving offence to any whilst firmly maintaining his convictions. His departure from this life, as my hon. friend has said, will be a severe loss to his friends. I sincerely appreciate the kindness of the remarks my right hon. friend has offered, especially with regard to Mr. Brown's family, and it will be my privilege to convey to them the observations which have been made by the Prime Minister with regard to our late lamented friend and colleague.

On the order for the second reading of Bill No. 120, respecting the Conveyance of Letter Carriers on Electric Railways:

This Bill being controversial, and likely to take up some time, and everybody having an earnest and sincere desire for prorogation as soon as possible, I will ask the House to allow me to drop this Bill for this session. One of the purposes for which it was introduced has been attained. I do not dike to use harsh words, but we had difficulty in coming to an agreement with an important tramway company as to the conveyance of our letter carriers. They wanted a price which was out of the way, and we thought it was in the public interest to introduce legislation so that we could control that, as we control everything we ask the railway companies to do for us. I am happy to say, however, that we have made a temporary arrangement with the company which, though it cost almost double, will enable us to wait until next session, as legislation will not be needed for some ten or eleven months. I only desire the House to understand the situation. Our letter carriers have been transported over the electric tramways in Canada for a long time. When the arrangement was started, the letter carriers found this to be a great convenience to them. The arrangement did not necessitate any increase in the number of cars, and the companies consented to give the service for a very low price. Little by little they increased the price, until we have now reached this situation, that the tramway company which for some years got $8,000 asked this year $20,000. That created a situation which had to be met. Fortunately, as I say, we have made this temporary arrangement.
What is the price agreed upon?
We have come to the conclusion to give $15,000, instead of $20,000, which they asked.
That is for Montreal?
For Montreal.

In Toronto, how much?
Mr. COCHRANE,

I have succeeded in
coming to a very satisfactory arrangement with the Toronto company, who met the Post Office Department in a very reasonable way. Last week we signed an agreement with the company in Toronto for four years at the rate of $12,000 a year. Toronto has three hundred and fifty-five letter carriers and special delivery messengers, and, as the number is likely to increase, we are going to gain as the second, third, and fourth years come along. That figure, $12,000 a year or $1,000 per month, represents a little over $34 per head. In Montreal we have three hundred and eight letter carriers, for whom we are paying $50 per head. That is the price we are obliged to pay-I am using the words advisedly. We have been obliged to make that arrangement, otherwise our letter -carriers would have had to walk, and that is impossible in these days. But that arrangement is for only a year. I am prepared to enter into any arrangement wdth all the companies in Canada at the reasonable rate agreed upon between the Toronto company and the department.
. Mr. LEMIEUX:	What do we pay in
Quebec?
$42.50 per man.
What is the number of letter carriers there?

The total number is
sixty-five. We have another grievance, which we have not settled so far, with regard to Ottawa. Whilst we pay the prices I have just indicated in Toronto, Montreal, and Quebec, we pay in Ottawa the enormous price of $75 per head, and, though I have tried my best, I have not been able to induce the Ottawa company to do as the others have done.
How many carriers are there in Ottawa?

Eighty-seven. Comparing these prices the House will see how unreasonable some of these companies are. I do not want to go too far at the moment, but I hope that those people will realize that they should give us as good an agreement as the one we have with Toronto, without legislation being necessary. I hope that before next session we shall be able to agree, for I would prefer not to reintroduce this Bill if we can agree. I would have preferred not to have presented the Bill if we could have agreed. The railway and -tramways companies had a kind of understanding, which is now gone because Toronto and Quebec have agreed that they should not stand by it. The understanding was that they should ask -sixty dollars per -head. Toronto has now consented to this, and I hope that I shall be able to settle all the

other questions. Under these circumstances, I ask leave to withdraw the Bill.

How is it that Toronto
has more letter carriers than Montreal, a very much larger city?
The revenue of Toronto is much higher than that of Montreal. It is very much larger than that of any other city in Canada.
Is there any arrangement at present with tramway companies in the maritime provinces?
We have not much diffculty there. There is one point in the West-I do not like to mention it-where we have some difficulty, as we also have in Ottawa.
If you mention Ottawa, why do you not mention the other recalcitrant?

I have no objection
to mention it. It is the same company practically as the Ottawa company.

May I ask the Postmaster General if the opinion of the law department is that it is within the jurisdiction of this Parliament to pass an Act that would compel a provincial corporation to carry letter carriers at a rate to. be fixed by the Postmaster General?

This point came up, and before introducing this legislation I consulted the Department of Justice about it, because I had some doubts myself. The Department of Justice sent me an official answer telling me that there was no doubt that we had the right.

One of the last Bills
of my own administration as Postmaster General was similar to this. We had a Bill passed to give our inspectors and assistant inspectors the right to travel on the trains of any provincial -or federal railway company on the business of the department, and the Department of Justice agreed that it was within our jurisdiction.
Has the Postmaster General had the advice of the Department of Justice in regard to jurisdiction over municipally owned electric railways?

My question did not
go that far. It was about tramway companies having provincial charters. I do not think I asked about municipally-owned tramways.
Would there be any difference?
I do not think there would be.
I cannot see any difference.

The Ottawa company
has a Dominion charter, if I am not mistaken.

The Ottawa company has, I think, a Dominion charter.

This work, commenced five or six years ago, is an earnest endeavour to connect the small harbour with the sea, in order to make a boat harbour for fishermen in that part of the county of Victoria. So far the work has not been very successful. Two piers were built extending out at each side, but the minister will have to extend those piers further to keep the stones and gravel from filling in the bottom of the harbour. I think it 'will be necessary to extend the piers.

The recommendation of
the engineer is for excavation and some extension to the piers.

This work has been rendered necessary because the formeT wharf was carried away by the ice when it broke up in the spring. The wharf is near the Intercolonial railway station and it is of great public service, especially to the people from the island, who land there.
I hope the minister will see that the money shall be expended during the summer.

The proposed wharf will
be 174 feet long extended to 11 feet at low water. I think it is about the same size as the former one.

The work is under contract; the contract price is $119,500.

the Nova Scotia Construction Company, and it has been transferred to Falconer & Macdonald of Halifax.
Caribou Island-raising causeway, &e., $6,400.

Does the minister
propose to spend $6,400 this year, and for what purpose? Will the work be done by contract or by day labour?
It is proposed to carry on the work by day labour owing to the difficulties in the way. It will be done this year.
What are the difficulties?
The work varies. One part is the raising of the causeway, and the other is something else, so that it would be difficult to do it by contract.

This is simply a permanent connection between the island and the mainland. Is there any defined time, or is it simply a case of putting in stone and earth in a desultory fashion, because that would be very unsatisfactory? I am anxious that this work shoulcf be done properly. The department should formulate a Mr. LAW.
plan in connection with it, and call for tenders.

The work for the present fiscal year consists in repairing and pointing the brush protection work on the seaward side; placing brush and stone and raising the lower part of the causeway to the level of twelve feet three inches above high water: During the year 1911-1912 about $1,000 was spent in placing some brush there and raising and repairing the roadway.

It is not very satisfactory to appoint a foreman and to employ men in the vicinity to haul stone and earth in a desultory way. This work has reached the stage that the department, before they expend any more money, ought to have a plan which would involve the permanent completion of the work. I want to urge upon the minister to have a work out of which the country will get full service, and which will mean the completion of proper connection between the island and the mainland.

We are taking a note of it, and will see that it is done.

Yes.
Devil's island-extension of breakwater,

This is a wharf on one of the arms of Bras d'Or lake. It is important because we are getting a boat to

ply between North Sydney and this place. What does the minister propose to do with this $2,600?

The approach to the wharf, which consists of brush and stonework covered with gravel, requires some replacing of the brush and stone that is broken down. It is a pretty large work, and we have a further amount in the supplementary estimates. It will probably be completed in two years.

I call the minister's attention to the necessity of making some repairs to the boat shelter at Lismore. This shelter was constructed four or five years ago and has been of great advantage to the fishermen of that part of the country. But' it was injured by storm last year, and has been allowed to fall into bad repair. It is an absolute necessity that it should be kept in good shape. Will the minister be good enough to see that the present condition of the work be inquired into and take the responsibility of preserving it ?

The chief engineer will take a note of it.

This is a very important point, and these repairs are much needed. Will this work be done by day labour or will tenders be asked for ?
This is simply for repairs and renewal of certain parts and is made up of small items. I am afraid it will have to be done by day labour.

I am not afraid of it, because the minister can get good men to do the work, and I only hope that he 362i
will instruct his engineers that it should be done as soon as possible.
/
Feltzen South-breakwater in Spindler'e Cove, $10,000.
Where is the work to be located-upon the site selected two years ago ?
Yes, on the same location as originally asked for.

Some three years ago tenders were asked for, for the construction of this work at a certain point. The lowest tenderer was one O. H. Ham. Yes, it is for repairs.

I think by day work.
Hantsport and Walton wharfs, $20,000.

Why are these
braoketed ? Are they close together .

Yes.
Harbour au Bouche-repairs to wharf,

repairs.

25,000	yards.

I want to impress
upon the minister the fact that this place is on a coast which is entirely exposed to the Atlantic, and that it is only during the mildest and warmest part of the season that any dredging can be done there. In the fall or spring, it is absolutely impossible to face that shore with a dredge.

manent character, will be inadequate. I hope the minister will take up this matter with confidence and a determination to put it through. The conditions described by my hon. friend are so imperative that they require immediate action.

due consideration and investigation, were put into the estimates of the year 1910-11. I must make a general remark about expenditures in Nova Scotia and my part of the country. who are aware that these expenditures in Nova Scotia are highly necessary, and that it was improper for the hon. member to make the vicious attack he did. I am not speaking for one side or the other; whichever party is in power it is necessary these expenditures should be made. I was trying for a great many years to get a harbour at Dingwall, in Victoria county, an important place, and after a struggle of many years we had an amount put in the estimates of 1910 and 1911. I am sorry that item has been dropped. There was another item in the estimates to help the fishermen out at Meat Cove and another for a breakwater at Cape Dauphin, and another item to help another fishing village at a place called Point Acoui. For some reason or other, which I never have been able to discover, those items have been dropped from the estimates. I am sorry for that. The minister will understand that the only way we have to compete with the American fishermen, who have large vessels outsidt the three-mile limit, and who sometimes come within the three-mile limit, is to have good sized boats that they can get out from these breakwaters. That is the reason why we are looking for those breakwaters and small harbours along the coast, so as to enable our fishermen to have goodsized boats. I am pleased to tell the minister that wherever we have a decent harbour our fishermen are getting good, large, gasoline boats and are able to compete with the Yankee fishermen, and go out in rough weather to share in the harvest of the sea. If the minister will look into t'he records of the department lie will find that his officers have reported in favour of these places I have mentioned. I am sorry that on the change of Government these items were dropped from the estimates, and I hope the minister will restore them and proceed with the work.

The commission reports:
That persons, who put in what are ostensibly competitive tenders, frequently have an understanding with each other in advance, as to what prices each shall bid, is quite evident on the face of the tenders themselves. In 1907, tenders were called for dredging at Midland and Waubaushene, and the Canadian 'Dredge and Construction Company, and the Penetanguishene Dredge Company each put in separate tenders for the work to be done at each of these two points, the tender of one company being the lower of the two at Midland, and the tender of the other company being the lower at Waubaushene. Is it contemplated that there should be a dam put across_ the Niagara river at the foot of Lake Erie in order to keep the water of the lake up to a certain specified level ?
That has been suggested aind the idea of this commission is to make us a report upon it so that we will know whether it is feasible or not.
Is Mr. Coste acting as engineer for the Deep Waterways Commission?

Yes, he is supposed to
be acting, but he is away now.

His idea was to put
submerged dams in the Niagara river. Gan the minister give ns any information sa to what is being done in regard to that?

Who are the members
of that commission? This is the commission that was composed of American members and Canadian members, is it not?

No, this commission is composed of Sir George Gibbons, Mr. Coste and Mr. Stewart. You are referring to the International Waterways Commission. That does not come under my department.
River St. Lawrence and Great Lakes Waterways Commission, $49,000.

What commission is
that?

This item has been in the estimates for some time and we have not been able to get the commission appointed, but we hope to shortly. This is the commission that was practically arranged for by my predecessor in appointing Mr. McLeod and Mr. Surveyor of Montreal. Mr. McLeod found it impossible to

act and give his whole time to the work. It is very desirable to secure him as head of the commission. He was here a few days ago and he informed, us that he hopes shortly to be able to give us a decided answer, as to whether or not he will be able to devote practically all his time to this work.

Yes, he is in McGill
University.

As I understand, they are to make an investigation of the St. Lawrence, the powers upon it and the effect of the development of these powers upon navigation. What portion of the St. Lawrence will their work cover?

All the way from Montreal to lake Ontario and all over. You can understand the difficulty which confronts the department. We have selected Mr. McLeod, Mr. Suveyer and Mr. CoutlSe of the department.

There is this difficulty connected with getting a report with regard to power in one locality only: You might send your departmental engineers to get a report upon the effect of the development of a water power in one locality. The commission is the only means of getting the information.
That is the idea.
The deepening of the canal through to Montreal is a pretty big problem in relation to the water supply in some of the lakes.

This extends their power to make an examination of the lakes tributary to the St. Lawrence river, so that they may have the widest possible power to examine into these questions.
Slides and booms generally, $5,000.
Mr.. GRAHAM: I have a complaint to make. An employee of the Government in South Renfrew took a very active part in the election, on the wrong side, of course for me, but on the Conservative side. I

Land and cable telegraph lines-Lower St. Lawrence and maritime provinces, $5,000.

Some years ago, Mr. Pugsley, when Minister of Public Works, granted to my old constituents in the Magdalen Islands a cheap rate for telegraph letters, between Meat Cove and the Magdalen Islands. That was a great boon to the people, who are cut off from communication with the outside world for several months in the winter. The Government sent this sum- ' mary by wireless and sometimes by cable, and it was supposed to be an unbiassed and non-partisan account of the news. I do not think so.
Have you a gentleman by that name in your department?
I do not know but I do not think so.

He was in the employ
of the Inland Revenue Department last year, and now I am told he is in the Interior Department. That same Mr. La-
Force is now the secretary of a commission nominated by the Department of the Interior to make investigation as to immigration to the province of Quebec. He is the

same man who has been charged in the newspapers in Quebec as having tried to bribe the Rev. Ivanhoe Caron to make him testify against Mr. Devlin's department in the provincial Government. This is entirely new to
me. I have never heard of Mr. LaForce that I know of, but I shall be pleased to draw to the attention of the minister in charge of the department in which he is, the remarks that have been made.
Telegraph lines-construction of line from Athabasca Landing to Fort McMurray, $7,700.

In so far as the loop to which my hon. friend refers is concerned, there should be no difficulty in arranging that. I shall undertake to have it provided. Do these Government
lines pay for themselves, or nearly so? I can understand that lines in not very thickly populated districts would hardly pay as well as lines where the population is more dense.

Can the hon. Minister
of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) tell us if the communication or exchange of telegrams between the Marconi company and the land lines has been iquite satisfactory. I have not heard any complaint at all in regard to it, and I have not paid much attention to it.
Riviere du Loup (Fraserville)-wharf improvements, $50,000.

around the wharf or in the river leading up to the town?

Department of Inland Revenue-salaries, $114,050.
Who is the deputy minister?
There is no deputy minister. Mr. Gerald has been superannuated since last October. The acting deputy minister is Mr. W. Himsworth. We expect to appoint a deputy shortly.
When does the hon. minister expect to appoint a deputy minister? The office has been vacant for quite a long time.
We expect to appoint one shortly.
It has been intimated that my hon. friend is keeping that office for one of the members of the House.
I think my hon. friend is mistaken. I have never heard -the name of any member of this House mentioned in connection with that.
The name of the hon. member for i'lslet (Mr. Paquet) has been mentioned.

No application has been received from any member of the House.
Mr. GAUVREAU.
When my hon. friend wants to make a promotion, how does he do it? That has to be done upon the recommendation of the deputy minister.
The recommendations are made by the minister upon the advice of the acting deputy.

Mr. Chairman, will the Minister of Inland Revenue allow me to give him my opinion? He is looking for a deputy minister. Why, there is one already found. Mr. Laflamme, the present secretary of the Department, ought to be appointed to that important office. It is not necessary that I should praise him.
Mr. Laflamme is a French Canadian who has a fine record in journalism. As such he has met with great success in the New England States and in Canada.
From what I know, Mr. Laflamme would be fully qualified to act as deputy minister. I know that the appointment of French Canadians should be based on efficiency. I will not insist any more than I should upon the fact that, as a distinct race, we are entitled to a certain proportion in the Civil Service. Efficiency should be first of all taken into consideration. Other, considerations being equal, should we not happen to have among deputy ministers the representation to which we are strictly entitled, when there is a vacancy to which one of our own people might fairly have a claim, I would recommend this gentleman to the kind consideration of the Government.
I believe that should the hon. minister appoint Mr. Laflamme he would have an efficient and upright deputy minister. I take the liberty of recommending him.
Although I am not a believer in Mr. Laflamme's political views, I feel bound to admit that he would do credit to the office of deputy minister.

I thank the hon. member for Rouville for the good suggestion he makes in connection with the future deputy minister. Mr. Laflamme has been secretary of the department for over nineteen months. He certainly is a well qualified man and I shall take note of the hon. gentleman's recommendation.
Salaries of officers and inspectors of excise, and to provide for increases depending on the result of excise examinations, $551,807.
Mr. -OARVELL: There is an increase here of $43,000 which, compared with the $508,000 of the previous year, is an increase of eight per cent or nine per cent in the salaries. How is it that there is such an enormous increase depending on examinations?

The number of officers
has been largely increased on account of the increase of revenue. These men will. | receive their regular increases after they pass their examinations.
How many are there?

There are the inspectors
of the inland revenue districts and of all collectors, deputy collectors and excise officers. Their regular increase is statutory under excise regulations.
I am told that there are some offices which should be closed because the revenue has largely decreased, and is exceeded by the expenses of the office.

I do not think my hon.
friend is well informed. The revenue has not decreased; on the contrary, it has increased generally.
An officer has been appointed at Victoriaville, the former member for Drummond and Arthabaska, and I am told that he goes to his office only once a week.

I can cite a worse case than that. About four years ago it was decided to abolish the office of collector of inland revenue at Woodstock, for the simple reason that there was nothing for him to do. There was at one time some business in the collection of the revenue on liquors, but fortunately no liquors are now sold in the county of Carleton. The Scott Act has been enforced there for many years, no liquor is bought or sold, and consequently there was nothing for the officer to do. The predecessor of my hon. friend came to me some three years ago and said he would have to abolish the office. I begged as hard as I could for retention of the office; the officer was an old man seventy-six years of age and had served for something like thirty-five years. I agreed with him, however, that when that officer died there should be no further appointments made. By some means or other-I never knew the modus operandD-certain fees were paid by some of the officials to retain the bonded warehouse as a justification of the retention of the office. When the old official died, somewhere about eight or nine months before the late Government went out of power, I had plenty of friends who were willing to take upon themselves the burden of filling this office, because there was $300 a year attached to it, and nothing to do, but, according to the agreement I made with the former Minister of Inland Revenue, no appointment was made, and the office was abolished. I am satisfied that my hon. friend will find in his department records to show that that office was not to be filled. About two months after this Government came into power the position was filled and I am told that the appointee, a Mr. Brown, was given a salary of $400 a year. Mr. Brown was a good Tory worker, and he had to get something. He wanted the post office, but that had to be given to somebody else, and he was given the position of collector1 of excise at $400 a year. That was not bad enough,, for they have since appointed	another man as some kind of an inspector. He is a man named Clark, and he is getting $300. Of course he is a Tory. He is a very respectable old gentleman of seventy-five or seventy-six years of age. He does not do any harm, but I am just as sure he does not do any good. My hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx) thinks he has a bad case, but I think the case I have cited is a great deal worse than his. Two officials have been appointed since my hon. friend took office and they have nothing to do, and $700 is paid out to good Tory heelers. Perhaps my hon. friend will explain how this happened.

The
minister seems to be rather slow in giving explanations. There is an increase m this item of $43,870 or about ten per cent. I think it is due to the House and to the country that the minister should give his reasons for the increase. The suggestion is made that it is owing to the fact that numerous office seekers have to he provided for, and that this is how provision is made. I found a case in a return which was brought down by the Minister of Inland Revenue.
Is that the case of Chisholm?

Yes. I asked for a return of all the papers and documents in connection with the dismissal of Donald Chisholm and the appointment of his successor. I had inquired previously whether a successor had been appointed. When the former preventive officer was dismissed, there appeared to be no reason for his continued existence, and there seemed to have been no reason for his existence for many years before he was dismissed. When I asked for the information, the minister stated that he had dismissed Chisholm on representations made to him by persons whose statements he had reason to trust. He rather evaded the question, and did not give me much information. But I persisted in my inquiries, and in his kind good natured way he came and asked me what further information I wanted. After speaking to him, he kindly brought down certain papers and among them a memorandum dated Ottawa, February 10, 1912, relative to the dismissal of Donald Chisholm, temporary preventive offioer in the Pictou division. You will observe Mr. Chairman, that this man was only a temporary preventive officer. The memorandum says that Donald Chisholm was temporarily employed on 24th December, 1896. I may explain that about that time there was a certain amount of illicit distilling in some sections of the county and I in the adjoining county of Pictou, and it

was considered necessary that an officer should be appointed, and Chisholm was appointed. The officer who had held the appointment prior to 1896 removed from the district or died. When Mr. Donald Chisholm was appointed a number of people felt there was no necessity for the appointment of such officer, and he was appointed only temporarily. Though there was no real reason for his continuance in the office, in later years his services were retained, the explanation being just the same as that suggested by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in reference to the case in his county. Chisholm was a very respectable old gentleman, an honest conscientious fellow who was esteemed by everybody in the community in which he lived, and it was expected that in a short time the office would be done away with. The salary he received was only $200, and it was thought that perhaps his retention of the position would be a deterrent of any further distilling in the district. The memorandum brought down by the minister states that at the time of his dismissal he was seventy-two years of age. There are some men who at seventy-two are old in vigour, as well as in years, and some who are not. Let us suppose that this man who had to deal with moonshiners was really old. The suggestion is made that he should have been dismissed many years before, but his services were not dispensed with until 1st November, 1912. Let us see what his services consisted of. The memorandum sets forth that during sixteen years he took part in five seizures. The seizures were initiated by E. P. Fraser, the very efficient collector of customs in Pictou, who has jurisdiction over the whole eastern portion of Nova Scotia. Chisholm took part in five seizures, three in 1897 and two in 1896. The records of the department show that after 1897 he did no work whatever. The fact of the matter is that the curse of illicit distilling of whiskey disappeared shortly after Mr. E. P. Fraser initiated his crusade against it, and possibly the fact that Mr. Chisholm was a local man had a deterrent effect upon the moonshiners. However, being an old and very respectable gentleman, he was continued in office from year to year, although, as I have shown, there was really no necessity for his being kept in the position. When I read the minister's memorandum I thought that it was because a preventive officer was no longer required that his services had been dispensed wiffi, but to my amazement I found that tEe minister appointed a new man.
A young man.

He dismissed Chisholm because there was nothing to do.
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
Because he was doing nothing.

Because there was nothing to do. No man, Grit or Tory, will venture the assertion that there has been any illicit distilling there in recent years. As a matter of fact, the criticism directed against the Liberal party and against myself in this connection was because this man was kept in office. It was said that we were simply keeping him there to provide a salary for a respectable old gentleman. The minister, and every officer in his department, knows that there was no necessity for this officer's services after 1897, but he has appointed a successor, and given him a salary of one hundred dollars more than the previous officer received, an increase of fifty per cent and he did this in the face of his own records. Where did my hon. friend get any justification for appointing a new officer? It was not because such an officer was needed. My hon. friend got his authority by appointing a food inspector. Think of it, a food inspector. A food inspector is needed there just as much as a newly born baby needs a beefsteak, to quote Gadsby, or a fifth wheel to a cart. I would like to know what food he has inspected since his appointment, or what food he will ever inspect. It is the most absurd thing. It would have been a perfectly proper thing for the minister to have dispensed with the services of Donald Chisholm when the present Government came into power. He expected that, and everybody else expected it, but the idea of appointing a successor to him is preposterous. It cannot be characterised as anything but a small steal out of the public treasury to provide for a man who is a good, active partisan. Why was this man appointed? Because he was a good active partisan, and for no other reason for no one can suspect him of having any qualification for a food inspector even if such were needed there. We have heard a great deal about men being dismissed for partisanship. Charity covers a multitude of sins it is said; but partisanship covers every excuse for needless dismissals and appointments. Charity cannot cover as wide a range as what is called partisanship. This thing covers everything discreditable to the present Government. It is illimitable in the extent to which it is worked. They bring this charge of partisanship against men who have given faithful service for the salaries they have received, and make it cover their sins of tyranny and injustice. This memorandum states that this man was 72 years old at the time of his dismissal, that he was appointed at a salary of $200, that his services were dispensed with on the 1st November, 1912, and that during the sixteen years he was employed, the records

^how that he took part in five seizures- three in 1897 and two in 1896. There seems to be no doubt at all that they had an ample excuse -for dismissing that man independently of any charge of partisanship. What is the explanation of it? The minister knew that this man, Donald Chisholm, should have been dismissed because his services were not required, but they wanted to find a place for this other man, Moses Delorey, who was recognized as an active political heeler, a man who, in season and out of season, had been engaged in active political work. Yet the minister appoints that man, knowing his record as an active partisan. Will he be removed from his present office on account of partisanship? No, he will not be. Recognizing that there was no need to appoint any person to this office, they said: We will have to get rid of this man on some other ground, not because he is too old, not because he is not needed, but we will have to specify something else, and therefore we find in this memorandum:
His removal was caused by political partisanship as will be seen by copies of affidavits attached.
Who gave that evidence? Has the minister any conscience at all?
