speechtext: Order.

If I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, I will withdraw that and ask what kind of a conscience he has. We expect something from him. All you have to do is to look at him. You will see an honest countenance; you will see a man who will not be disposed to allow the public treasury to be looted.
Mr. GRAHAM Or diluted.

You will see a man who in a person embodies the virtues of good nature and honesty. That is why I appeal to him particularly. Of course, if it were the hon. Minister'of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) or the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) it "would be different; they are men who are out for political scalps they are playing the game, all the time. They care not, they are bold, they are brazen, and they will defy public opinion afterwards. The Minister of Inland Revenue will not do that; he is seemingly honest, frank and sincere. I find that on March 21, 1912, in answer to some questions that I put to the minister, ' Hansard,' page 5819, the minister laid d-own this rule:
If a member states that he is aware of his own personal knowledge than an officer has been guilty of offensive partisanship, we shall probably decide to dismiss him without investigation.
This is a careful minister; he is not too bold. He says that we shall probably dismiss him without further investigation Then he says further:
If the charge is by the member on his own personal knowledge we will act on it

Quite properly too.
If it is by the defeated candidate, who gives sufficient facts and proofs, affidavits and so forth, to convince me that there is reason to act and dismiss, I will dismiss; and each case will be decided on its merits.
Not on political expediency. I want to admit that in so far as I am concerned I never recommended the dismissal of that man, Donald Chisholm. I must plead guilty to the fact that I should have recommended his dismissal some years ago. But the circumstances were extenuating; he was an old man, he was very much respected in the community, his home was open to everybody who travelled through that section of the country, and I never had the heart to recommend his dismissal in his old age. True, in so far as his services were concerned, they could have been dispensed with years ago as there was nothing for him to do. But now the minister dismisses him, turns around and appoints another man in his place and gives this other man an extra salary by stating that he is a food inspector. How many government food inspectors are there in the province of Nova Scotia? What are their duties, and how long are they to be retained? These are questions that I would like to have the minister answer.
Does the hon. gentleman mean preventive officers or food inspectors?

I am speaking of pre-ventitive officers who are salved by the title of food inspectors, preventive officers who are absolutely unnecessary, whose duties ceased long ago, and who, upon being appointed, are given an extra salary of $100 under the excuse that they are to act as food inspectors. What are the duties of these food inspectors? The memorandum says:
Mr. Chisholm was replaced by Mr. Delorey who was appointed preventive officer and inspector of food, from the 12th December, 1912, for which he is receiving $200 as preventive officer and $100 as food inspector.
I wish, Mr. Chairman, to draw your attention to the fact that this appointment was made a short time previous to the local bye-election in the county of Anti-gonish, but the appointment was concealed from the public until after the election was over and until I made inquiry in this House, by reason of the fact that the Conservative machine down there had to use this office and many other offices to try to bait the people along. They not only instituted a system of terrorism in that constituency as to existing officials

but they tried to give the people to understand that there were new offices to be filled and they promised one of these new offices to every man whom they thought to be doubtful. This man, Moses Delorey, was not doubtful, but he was somewhat disgruntled. He had worked long and faithfully for the Conservative party, he had done good work and they rewarded him by giving him this office of preventive officer at a salary of $200 with $100 extra as food inspector. Will the minister tell me why he appointed a food inspector down there, and why, if he was going to make the appointment, he did not make it at some place where such an officer might be of some use. Why was he not appointed in the shire town where there are butcher stalls and where meat and other kinds of food are being exposed for sale? Instead of that, he appointed him in-a very fine district-I have not a word to say against it-but in a district where there is no particular business done.

I am really at a loss to know why the hon. member for Antigonish takes so much interest in the fate of that Mr. Chisholm. I do not know if he is a relation of his, but any way he is greatly interested in him. At all events, I have judged proper to dismiss Mr. Chisholm, because complaints have been made against him.

I will explain to you now; that he is not. The only relative I have had in the Government service was a brother who was the station master an Heatherton on the Intercolonial railway and he was the only station master from Halifax to Montreal who was dismissed. His offence was that he voted for his only brother. He was quite satisfied to take his medicine if that rule was to be applied and the principle was to be laid down that to the victors belong the spoil, but it is rather a significant circumstance, and rather a reflection upon the man who recommended the dismissal, as well as upon the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), that the only man singled out for such treatment was the brother of a member. The father of the man who recommended that dismissal, the father of Senator Girroir, was postmaster for many years in Antigonish county, and I was -asked to dismiss him, but I said no, I will never be guilty of doing such a mean, contemptible thing.

In any case, Mr. Chisholm was a temporary employee since December 24, 1896, as a preventive officer. He was an old man whose only occupation was to draw his salary.
When I was asked to dismiss him, he was accused of having taken an active part in the last election. Mr. Girroir has declared Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
th-at himself in a personal letter which runs as follows:
I have personal knowledge that Mr. iChis-holm at each election spent considerable time in visiting his friends with w-hom -he had influence in canvassing them to vote for the Liberal candidate. He has always been outspoken in the Liberal cause and even meet-*, ings of the organization have been held at his house. He was, during the last election, a member of the Liberal organization committee for the polling district of Tracadie. I would recommend that 'Mr. Moses Delorty be appointed.
Are you reading from a letter of Mr. Girroir?

Yes.
On receiving that letter I asked the deputy minister for a report. I have received that report in which it is stated that Mr. Chisholm had been really a preventive officer since December 24, 1896, and that from that date up to 1911 he had done nothing else but drawing his salary of $200 a year. I have thought proper to dismiss him, giving as my reasons that he had not shown enough activity in the fulfillment of his duties. A long while after that, I was asked to appoint a new preventive officer, and I have appointed Mr. Delorey, and I gave him at the same time the charge of food inspector.
If Mr. Delorey does not show more activity than did Mr. Chisholm, his predecessor, I will dismiss him, on the necessary proofs.
Why have you increased his salary?

Because we have given
him a new employment, that of food inspector, -and I may assure you that is no sinecure. That inspector is under the control of the analyst who often asks him for samples of foods which the inspector must send to the analyst's office. We are thus in a position to administer the law concerning the adulteration of food.
For that other function, I have given him an additional salary of $100 a year.

Has the minister nothing to say to the charge that he did not bring down the full return to the House? Why, that constitutes a contempt of Parliament.
' Mr. NANTEL:	There were contained in
that report all the documents which were on file at the department. Mr. Girroir's letter was private and confidential. I have not seen fit to produce it, and I don't believe I am obliged to do it, because it is a personal affair. But I have given communication of it to the hon. member.

If it is a personal and
private letter it has no business to be read in the House.
And the minister has no business dismissing a man on a personal letter.
It was not on the regular file.
The minister has read a private and confidential letter to the House and that letter must go on the official record.
I have no objection.

The minister does not
appear to realize the situation; if he does he has been guilty of contempt of an order of the House.

Report
him to the Governor General.

The House ordered that this complete return should be brought down and the minister brought down the return on his responsibility, and it is not a complete return, and the Prime Minister should ask for his resignation.
The report I have submitted to the House comprised all the documents which were in the possession of the deputy minister.
What is the date of Mr. Girroir's letter?

The 27th June. Later on my hon. friend (Mr. Chisholm) asked me for some information. I am quite sure that I have given a copy of that letter. That I do not positively recollect, but I am sure I gave him the contents of that letter.

I will
explain that. The minister may be in good faith; he is in good faith in making that statement, and he probably believes it. But this is the explanation; when I moved for the papers in the House and they were brought down, the papers did not contain all the details that I required. The papers did not make any reference to Senator Girroir. By reference to ' Hansard ' you will find that I asked on whose recommendation Donald Chisholm had been dismissed, and the minister replied on representations made to him verbally and on affidavits he had received. When I put the further question by whom these recommendations were made the minister refused to give me that information, or at all events gave me what I considered an unsatisfactory answer. Then I raised a question of privilege and I complained the minister was not giving the information he was required to give, even to an humble back-bencher if you wish to call me so. The minister then came over to me and said: What further information are you asking; what are you complaining about. I said:	I want to know
from you who was it gave you the oral information, and what is the nature of it, and the minister said: Mr. Girroir told me certain things. I said: Are these in writing, and the minister said, no.
Did I not send you a copy of that letter?

The minister did not send me a copy of the letter, and the minister stated to me that the representations made to him by Senator Girroir were oral, and that is precisely why I brought the matter up to-night to see if I could not entrap the minister and get the facts. All the minister has to do is to look up ' Hansard,' and he will see that my statement is correct.
I will look into the matter.

I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there is no member of this House who would like to be more liberal to the feelings or prejudices of any member of this House than I am. I am proud of the fact that hon. members who speak the French language are privileged to speak that language in the House. I take pride in , the fact that hon. members

in this House speak the French language and have the privilege of expressing their views .in that language. I protest that it is receiving money under false pretenses for a minister of the Crown to be holding a portfolio of the Crown and to refuse to answer an English-speaking member in a language that he can understand. The hon. minister can speak the English language. I am an English-speaking member, who is under the disability of not being able to understand the French language. I must, therefore, put up with that disability when an hon. member is speaking in French; but, when a minister of the Crown, who is discharging the responsibilities of his office, is speaking to me in this House, I have a right to be addressed in a language that I can understand. I protest that, when the right hon. gentleman who leads this House selected his Nationalists, he selected Nationalists who evidently cannot speak the English language or who decline to show the courtesy of speaking to English-speaking members in a language that they can understand and of giving them the opportunity of criticising if necessary their conduct. I make this protest, not in the slightest heat, and with every respect to the rights of hon. gentlemen to speak the beautiful French language which I regret exceedingly I cannot speak or understand. I submit, if a French member addresses an English minister in this House and if that English minister can speak French, that he is not treating the French member properly, if the latter cannot speak English, if he addresses him in a language that he cannot understand.

I protest against the hon. gentleman's protest. Both languages are official. I have the right to speak ip French to my hon. friend. If he does not understand French, that is not my fault. I have the right to speak French in this House as much as any other hon. member has the right to speak English to a French member who is not supposed to understand English. When a French member from Quebec is obliged to express himself in French to an English member of the Cabinet who does not understand French, nobody complains. I have a perfect right to do the same. I protest against your own protest.

I am very pleased with
the result of the protest made by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). It at least shows the Opposition and the members of this House that the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue can, when he desires to do so, speak the English language and speak it very fluently. As a matter of right, I would be the last man in this House of Commons to say that a member has not the right to speak the French language. It is a right which is very sacred, Mr. McKenzie.
a right of which we Freneh-Ganadians are very proud and very jealous; but I certainly do not think that the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue was justified in giving the answer he did to the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie), especially after the example which was set for him by the right hon. the leader of the Government. Upon several occasions the right hon. the Prime Minister, who certainly does not speak French better than the hon. member speaks English, has been addressed by hon. members on this side of the House in the. French language and very courteously has answered them in that language. I think that the hon. minister misunderstood what he calls our protest. We are not speaking about the question of right whatever; we are speaking of a question of courtesy; and, as he is able to speak the English language so fluently, I think it would be very much better for every one concerned if the deliberations in committee were carried on in English, and if he would show the English-speaking members the same courtesy that the Prime Minister has on several occasions shown to French speaking members on this side of the House.

I did not speak French as a lack of courtesy to the hon. member for Antieonish (Mr. Chisholm). I spoke the French language because it was easier for me to'do so. I regret very much not being as conversant with the English language as my hon. friend is.

That ia not the point. The hon. member for Cape Breton is referring to the constitutional right and duty of a Cabinet Minister to speak in either language when he is able to speak in both languages. A minister should speak in the language in which he is addressed when he has command of both tongues.

I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue had any thought or intention of showing discourtesy to the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) when he undertook to answer his questions in his mother tongue. All hon. members know that the French and the English languages are the official languages of this House. I was pleased to note that, when my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue answered my hon. friend from Antigonish in French, the latter apparently perfectly understood the hon. minister, and was able to make answer in the manner in which he did, so that I do not think that any injustice has been done or any attempt been made on the part of hon. gentlemen to show any sign of discourtesy. I trust that hon. members opposite will understand that no discourtesy was intended. We have had a very pleasant and useful day in carrying on the pub-

lie business. I hope * it will be continued for the balance of the evening. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Antigonish on his knowledge and understanding of the French language.

I am
sorry that not only my modesty but my ignorance prevents me from accepting the compliments paid to me by -the acting leader of the Government (Mr. Rogers). I regret to say that I do not understand French, although I can read it rather indifferently. In this case I had the benefit of an interpreter.
I want to direct the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue to page 440 of the Votes and Proceedings where he will find that an order was passed on January 29, for a copy of all letters, correspondence on file referring to the dismissal of Donald Chisholm, of Tra-cadie, in the county of Antigonish, as preventive officer. I ask him to look at the papers that were brought down; and I ask him if, in that light, he realizes his position in failing to respond to that Order of the House.

When the returns were
prepared by the deputy minister, the letter of Senator Girroir was not on the official file. When my attention was called to the fact by the hon. member for Antigonish, if I remember rightly, I asked him if he wanted that letter. I gave him the information and I am quite sure that I gave instructions to furnish him with that letter.
I have not got it.

I will verify that. I am quite sure that I gave instructions to furnish my hon. friend with the letter. That letter was in my private file; but it is not marked private, and I gave instructions to my officer to send it to my hon. friend. I am quite sure that the letter was addressed to him. Have you received that letter?

I did not receive the letter, so far as my memory serves me. In the conversation which I had with the Minister of Inland Revenue, he told me that Senator Girroir had made his representations orally. I had reason to believe that Mr. Girroir was at the bottom of this, and that is why I asked for the correspondence. What I object to is this, that the letter, which was not marked private had not been brought down with the other papers. There is1 no such letter on my file and I think I am pretty careful about keeping my papers together. But I would not contradict the minister when he says he sent it, for there are two of us by the same name, members in this House, and our letters sometimes go to the wrong man. Letters intended for the member for Inverness come to me and vice versa. Why was it not on file? What
kind of administration have we In this country? What confidence can the people have in the way affairs are administered when letters are left off these files as a mere matter of choice? This is not public business at all; it is secret, dangerous business that is going on.

Now that the minister has shown that he can talk fluently in either language, I would like him to answer in French or in English, I do not care. What is the use of making appointments in my town if the services of these officers are not required?
What appointments?

The two appointments
I spoke of, one at $300 and one at $400. What is the use, when there is nothing for these officers to do? One is Mr. Brown and the other is Mr. Clarke.

I join with the hon.
member for Red Deer, but I think that he has not gone far enough. The hon. member for Carleton said that not only was there no illicit manufacture of liquor, but he went further and said that there was no sale or use of it.

We do not know what illicit distillation means down there. No officer was ever appointed in New Brunswick for the purpose of keeping that down. The duty of the officer at one time was when the liquor was manufactured to put 't in the bonded warehouse and receive the duty on it.

I desire information concerning the appointment of the officer re-

ferred to by the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) a few moments ago, Mr. Gilbert, of Arthabaska. When was he appointed, what are his duties, and what is his salary?
Mr. Gilbert is collector of inland revenue for Drummond and Arthabaska; his salary is $600, and he was appointed to Teplace Mr. Poirier.
What is the revenue of the office?	_
I am not in a position to give that information to-night, but will make a note of the point and give it later.

Another bit of information, I should like to get is, whether this Mr. Gilbert is the same Mr. Gilbert, who was Nationalist candidate in the Drummond and Arthabaska byt-election in 1910. That was a very important by-election in the province of Quebec, in fact the minister said he changed his opinion at the time of that election. Since that date, and especially in the past few months, some members have gone so far as to say that there was a chance of an alliance between the Nationalists and the Liberals. Are we to understand that this Nationalist candidate in Drummond and Arthabaska has been appointed to office by this Government?
Mr. Gilbert is the same man. I made a mistake in saying that his salary is $600; I have ascertained that his salary is $800.
How often does he go to his office? I am told that he resides quite a distance from Vietoriaville, on his farm, and goes to his office very infrequently.
I am told that Mr. Gilbert keeps his office well. I have never received any complaint concerning him.

I have personal
knowledge of the facts, because I was living there for quite a while. Mr. Gilbert is farming on his farm at Stanford. He goes to the office when he is telephoned for.
This is the first complaint I have received concerning this officer. I will make a note of it, and if there is any irregularity I will try toi remedy it.

I do not complain
of it, so long as those who are in need of Mr. Gilbert do not complain.

I am told there are
quite a few offices that should be closed, the revenue not being sufficient to pay the expenses of the office. I have been told that this is that kind of an office.

I am informed that Mr. Gilbert makes his return very regularly to his chief, Mr. Benoit.
Mr. BOTVIN.	'

Have there been any
increases recently in the salaries of inland revenue officers in the city of Halifax?
I am not aware of any.

I desire to bring to the attention of the minister the case of Mr. Patrick Tompkins, who has been an officer of the department in the city of Halifax for the past twenty-five years. He happens to be a close personal friend of my own, but a political friend of the minister. A good many years before 1896, he was appointed to office by the Conservative Government. He was a strong Conservative then, and is the same to-day. He has been a most efficient officer. He has succeeded in capturing many of these distilleries that they have in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, and has done much to stamp out that business. Personally, I tried to get an increase in his salary from the late Government, but did not succeed. As a matter of fact, Mr. Tompkins came near being dismissed from office at one time on account of his political complexion. I do not care what his politics may be, he has been in the service a long time, and has always fulfilled his duty faithfully and well. He should receive more than his present salary, which, J. think, is $800 a year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know anything
about Mr. Tompkins' qualification. I really was not aware of his political opinions, but I have known him a long time, and I have believed him to be a very faithful and efficient officer. I remember years ago that I had occasion to note the .manner in which he performed his duties, and I entirely agree with what my hon. friend says as to his efficiency and devotion to duty.

Patrick Tompkins, third-class exciseman, was appointed on August 14, 1879. He his now receiving a salary of' $1,000, which is the maximum he is entitled to receive, because he has never passed an examination. I must say that the salaries of all these officials are certainly small, and I have thought of increasing them.

I am .glad that the
minister intends to increase the salaries of these officials. I do not know exactly whether he has made any increase in the salary of his official in the prosperous and growing town of Sydney. In Sydney, living is just as expensive as it is in Montreal or Toronto. When the late Government was in power, I was trying to get an increase in salary of this official, Mr. Macdonald by name, but I did not succeed in getting anything for him. I hope that my hon. friend the minister has done some-
115ao

thing for him, or has some intention of increasing his salary. I think he is receiving about $800, entirely too small a salary for anyone living in Sydney.
I have only one word to say. I would like to know from the hon. minister why Mr. Martin, of St. Arsene, has been dismissed and who has been appointed to take his place?
What is his name?

Elie Martin.
While the deputy minister is looking over his papers, in order to enable the minister to answer my question, I will ask him if he knows that at Riviere du Loup prohibition prevails, the dry regime is in force and there are no more licenses to sell liquor, wholesale or retail? I therefore warn the hon. minister that the man they have appointed, Mr. Frenette, has no revenue at all, although he is a married man and the father of a family. The salary he is receiving is pitiable. What I blame the Government for is that they have divided the office of collector, held by one Mr. Pelletier, an office which gave a man a decent living, but is not enough for two. Having divided it in two you simply have two men starving.
Although Mr. Frenette is one of my political opponents, I will readily give him the credit of -being an honest man, and I feel it my duty to ask the minister if, under the circumstances, he could not find somewhere else for him a position that would give enough to live upon. I am against dismissals, especially when women are the victims, and I am -always ready to help those who are in -want and who properly fulfil their duties. I believe the hon. minister is well disposed, so that I shall ask him whether he could not give Mr. Frinette another position with a proper salary that would enable him to earn his living.

That is very well
spoken.

As to Mr. Frenette, his
salary must be provided for, that is evident under the circumstances, because the position he is now occupying at Rivifere du Loup is a sinecure which brings him nothing. He will have to be transferred somewhere else, into another division, because there is nothing for him to do where he is.
As to Mr. Elie Martin, of St. Arsene, I have not the information just now to give an -answer to the hon. -member.
Can the hon. minister give us the name of the officer of his department in the city -of F-amham, which is situated in the Bedford division?
Have you his name?
I have not his name. I believe he took the place of a Mr. Porte-lance.
Is he a preventive officer?
No, I believe he is collector of excise, because there is a cigar factory in Farnham.

We have several officers
who are only temporary. I have not at the present moment the information required 'by my hon. friend. I am making a note of this and I will give it later on.
Adulteration of f-oo-d and the administration of the Act respecting fertilizers, -fraudulent marking and commercial feeding stuffs, $30,000.
Before this item is adopted, can the hon. minister tell me who is the food inspector in -the Bedford district?

I may say that all the
revenue officers are inspectors, according to-law but the chief inspector of that district lives in Montreal. As I just said, it is the duty of the revenue officers to see that this law is properly carried out.

Will the hon. minister tell me what is the salary paid to Mr. Van Antwerp, who is at the same time excise and weights and measures officer, whether he is a permanent officer or only working temporarily?
I am taking note of this.
Are all the food inspectors living in Montreal, and are they sent from there to all parts of the province?

No. The province is
separated into divisions and a certain number of inspectors reside in these respective districts.
Can the hon. minister tell me how many food inspectors there are in Nova Scotia, giving the number in each county if possible?
I will get the information for my hon. friend.	.

How many divisions are
there -and how many inspectors? The hon. minister might give me that information on supplementary estimates.
Yes.

Am I to understand that the minister will furnish the information later on ? If so, I would ask him to give the date of appointment of each of those food inspectors, and the names and addresses of the parties appointed.
Miscellaneous-distribution of parliamentary documents, $1,500.

Might I draw the attention of the leader of the House to a

question which has been put to me by several members? The distribution of parliamentary documents is made during the session in a very fair manner by the distributing officer, but several members would like to receive documents after the session is over. They have called at Mr. Davidson's office and have been informed that he would distribute the documents between sessions with pleasure, but that he does not enjoy the franking privilege after the session is over. It seems to me that when members require blue-books or other parliamentary documents, the franking privilege ought to be given to the distributing officer, so that those members who live at a distance could receive them after the session. Mr. Davidson says he is obliged to pay for the stamps necessary to send those documents. Perhaps the Postmaster General will take a note of that.

I do not know what my hon. friend's request would amount to. I have not heard of it before, but the matter will be taken up and considered. If it is simply a question of franking in sending out certain material, I do not think it would be very serious. Of course, there have been times when it appeared to the post office authorities that the franking privilege was being very much abused, and they naturally have to curtail the privilege as much as possible. However, this matter will be looked into, and if it is possible to meet the suggestion of my hon. friend, something will be done.

I would like to say a word concerning the distribution of blue-books during the session. In previous years we had a room called the ' blue book room,' where the blue books for the different members were left, and where they could be called for at any time, used in the members' rooms, or sent to their homes. I understand that that blue book room has been abolished, and the result is that during the present session we have had blue books piled on our desks and tables in the different rooms without knowing where they came from, or whether we had already got them or not. In certain instances several important reports have not pome to us at all, while we have been overwhelmed with other blue books for which we have no use. I think that the blue book room was a great convenience to all the members, and I regret very much that it has been abolished. Would it not be possible to have something of the same nature in use next year ?

Of course the Government are very anxious to provide hon. members with every facility in regard to obtaining all the information and all the books that are printed from time to time, Mr. LEMIEUX.
and if there is any mistake, or any delay, we will certainly be,' glad to remedy it.

Whilst we are on this subject I would like to call the attention of the French-speaking ministers to something which is not new, but which I hope will not happen again in view of the nomination made recently of ten new translators. To give an instance of the poor service we have had in the distribution of public documents or blue books, I may say that we have received only this, month the Auditor General's report in French for 1911-12. I understand that a radical change is about to take place, the Speaker and Deputy Speaker having arranged to appoint new translators, who, I am told, are all very competent. They have passed a Civil Service examination, and I understand they are to be appointed shortly. I hope that in the future we shall have the French blue books within a reasonable time.

That is one of the
reasons why the Speaker and the Committee of Internal Economy have come to the conclusion that instead of having the translations done all over the country, and the work consequently delayed, these new translators should be appointed to take care of the work. As the hon. member has said, I think we can rely on the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker to see to it that these translations are made within a reasonable time.

Have these translators
been appointed in order of merit?
They have been appointed by the Speaker, with the concurrence of the Committee of Internal Economy.

An examination was
held?
Yes.

I understand that no age limit was fixed before the examination was held. Candidates were invited to come to Ottawa to pass an examination, but, after the examination had been held, the commission fixed an age limit at forty years, I think, and some of the candidates who were over forty years of age, were among the first ten in the list of those who passed. I know one candidate who took fifth place, but he did not get an appointment because he was over the age limit.
The translators appointed were recommended by the commission.

What I find fault with
was that the age limit was fixed before instead of after the examination.

If my hon. friend
finds fault with the commission, there are probably a good many people who will agree with him.

I am told that these
appointments were made not by the Civil Service Commission, but by the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker, and the Committee of Internal Economy, and that they, and not the Civil Service Commission, fixed the age limit.

The Committee of
Internal Economy do not fix the age limit They make the appointments, but like the various departments of the Government, they have to take the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission. We have two commissioners. Sometimes they agree, and sometimes they do not. When they do agree, they make recommendations to the departments, and the appointments go through by Order in Council. In the present case, the appointments have been made by the Speaker with the concurrence of the Committee of Internal Economy.

The candidates in that
examination had to pay a fee of $8. Will the fee be remitted to those who succeeded in passing the examination, but who could not be appointed because they were over forty years of age?
I cannot tell my hon. friend that, but I might inquire and let him know.

Before the item relating to the distribution of blue books is passed, I would suggest to the leader of the House that the whole system of distribution be reorganized. I would suggest, not another blue book room, but a proper organization of the present room. It is a common thing for members to go to the distribution office, and to be told they cannot get the book they ask for. The messenger has to search in various offices around the city to find small publications issued by the departments of the Government. Sometimes he comes back after a long search without the documents required, and sometimes we are told that these documents can be obtained at the King's Printer's office or at other places. I see no reason why a distribution office should not be so organized that every publication of the Government would be available to every member on application. I would suggest that the Government look into the question with the view of reorganizing the system and of placing it under proper management, so that when members ask for any publication of the Government at the distribution office, the officers m charge would be able to find it.

The statement made by my hon. friend is a serious one. If any
officer in the employ of the Government has been guilty of refusing to give consideration to members-

I am not suggesting that anyone has been guilty of that. I say that the distribution room is not furnished with all the publications of the Government. I think the officers in the distribution room are very efficient; they do everything they can to find publications required by members. But the system is such, that a good many publications are not under the control of the distribution staff at all.

If the statement of my
hon. friend is correct, the matter should certainly be looked into, and we will endeavour to do so with the view of rectifying any grievance that may exist. The room to which he refers should be supplied with every blue book and Government publication. I will take note of the matter and endeavour to see that it is put right.

I wish to make a simple request to the leader of the House. Would it not be possible in future for members to obtain a few more copies of ' Hansard ' than they get now? Each member gets three copies, but 1 would be very glad to get more. The expense of printing a few more copies would not amount to very much.

The question of the number of copies of ' Hansard ' available to members is entirely in the hands of thet Debates Committee. They have the matter in hand, and as my hon. friend well knows, it has been the practice for a very long time to allow only so many copies to each member. So far as I understand the question from the information I have, it might be a good thing for the public business of this country if we had less ' Hansard ' than we have.
Hear, hear.

However, I might be mistaken in that. At the same time, the matter of which my hon. friend complains is entirely in the hands of the Debates Committee, and I have no doubt they will take a note of what he has said, and if they choose to find a remedy there will be no objection on this side of the House.

I
would suggest that the Debates Committee take into consideration the advisability of abolishing ' Hansard.'

I quite agree with the statement made by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton. I do not think that the Minister of Public Works ought to grumble at the number of ' Hansards ' so much as at the fact that there is a ' Hansard ' at all. If he could get rid of ' Hansard ' entirely,

there might be something in his argument, but seeing that it exists, I do not see that it makes very much difference whether the number given to each member is three or six. This matter has come up a good many times, and I could never understand why the number should be restricted. But there seems to be a desire on the part of the Debates Committee to restrict the number of unrevised ' Hansards ' given to each member; for what reason I do not know, unless it be that ' Hansard ' is not perfect. But a member should be held responsible for what he says in the House, and I do not think he ought to be allowed to change ' Hansard ' to any great extent. I think the ' Hansard ' reports as a rule are pretty accurate, and I do not see why members should not have a reasonable number of co'pies, if they want them, to send to their constituents. Personally I would like to have more than three copies, and I think I am voicing the sentiment of many members on both sides of the House in saying so.
I do not send ' Hansard to my constituents, but I have been surprised at the number of requests for copies from people all over Canada. It has cost me probably $50 this session to send copies.

I would like to suggest to the minister that when he is looking into this matter he should try to find some means of avoiding the printing of so many parliamentary documents that none of the members want. They are piled on the desks and tables, and it has seemed to me that there was a great waste that might be avoided. I would .suggest that he deivse some system of supplying the documents that people generally want and that are not too heavy.

As my hon. friend can understand, it is very difficult for the officers who have matters of this kind in charge to decide what documents are more useful, acceptable, or desirable, than others. It would be very difficult for those officers to say that only a certain number of copies of a certain document should be printed, and that h certain number of another document should not be printed, though I presume they have some kind of rule which they follow in matters of that kind. I can quite understand that certain documents are not being made use of by members of the House, and that they accumulate and become practically useless. J do not know that that can be remedied, but it is a point that might well be con .sidered by those who have the matter in charge. It will be brought to their notice, and some saving might be made in the direction suggested.

The matter might be arranged by a circular form of application sent to each member to be returned to the Mr. CiRMEiLL.
distribution office asking for such blue books as he would want. Then the Government would only be required to supply a certain number. There are a number of blue books that I do not want at all, they are a nuisance to me and I cannot find room for them, while there are others that I would like to get more of.
Mr. (STANFIELD:	The printing committee at the last meeting took that matter up, and they are trying to provide some means whereby useless blue books shall not be sent to members.

I think it might be
worked out in that way. I would like a few more copies of some blue books and the cost would not be any more to the Government to give me what I need. There are certain blue books that are of interest to the people of my constituency, and others which are not required at all. I think we should have a chance to make some choice.

I think the difficulty
could be very easily gotten over if the distribution office upstairs were enlarged and if instead of the books being sent around to different members, as they are at the * present time, whether we want them or not, these reports were left in the blue book office to be called for by the members as required, at the end of the session. The officers of the different departments would very soon see how many books of each kind would be required, they could govern themselves accordingly in future years, and there would be a saving to the country in future. It would be much more satisfactory because there are a number of blue books that many members do not look at, and there are others of which they would like to have more than a limited supply.

That rulte might isuit
certain hon. gentlemen, but take for example the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham)-do you suggest that he would take the trouble to go around to the distribution office for a blue-book and take it with him?
It is not necessary to go around; all you have to do is to ring for a messenger.

However, there might be some advantage in the suggestion.
Public Archives-formerly voted under Art, Agriculture and Statistics, $35,000.

I would like to ask my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) if the Government has considered the succession to the late Mr. Roy, who for so many years was one of the archivists, one of the most distinguished men

of letters this country has produced, and who died a few weks ago. The other day, while I was attending the sittings of the Royal Society, they were discussing the question of a successor to Mr. Roy. I understand that a recommendation is generally made by the Committee on Archives. I hope the successor to Mr. Roy will be selected for his ability and not for his party affiliations. I will recall to my hon. friend that Mr. Roy was appointed by a Liberal government because he was a most competent man for that very important position. I know that if somebody has the ability in the Conservative party the position goes of right to him, but the Government should find the best man and give it to him. It is very important that Mr. Roy should be succeeded by a man of the highest ability. You may find somebody to succeed him but nobody to replace him.

Whilst I have no
authority to speak on the question, as the matter is in the Department of the Secretary of State, I acknowledge that what the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has said is perfectly true. The late, esteemed Mr. Roy had been a Conservative but he was appointed on account of his very great ability. Now that he is gone I can give my hon. friend the assurance that the appointment would be made with the same idea and the same end in view. Without giving any names for the moment, I may say that one gentleman who has been recommended, and highly recommended, by a very great many of the most influential men outside of politics will very likely get the appointment.

Has the amount of the
vote for the Archives been increased over what it was last year?

Mr. Fabre had been one of the ,most prominent men of our race. For a long time he has wielded a clever and alert ped in the service of Canada. As a literary man he certainly ranked among the best. His

The remarks just

There is this difference between the civil servant at five hundred dollars and the girl at three dollars a week. In the case of the civil servant at five hundred dollars, it is a question of getting efficient service; but in the case of the girl at three dollars a week, it is an absolute case of getting a livelihood. I think it would be a very proper thing for the Government to establish a minimum wage for their employees in the lower grades, because these are the employments in which the people concerned are not so circumstanced so that they can protect themselves by the formation of unions. Men in the higher classes of employment can and do protect themselves by the formation of unions, but it is the people in the lower classes of employment who cannot do so, and they should have such protection as the Government may be able to give them.

What attention has been paid to the requirements of Ontario in' the propaganda that has been carried on in the United States in regard to immigration?
I see by the Auditor General's report that last year there was considerably over half a million dollars spent in the United States for promoting immigration to Canada and about a quarter of a million dollars spent in Great Britain. Is there any attention beind paid to the unoccupied lands in Ontario in the advertising that is being done in the United States? Is there any effort being made to colonize the lands in Ontario or is the effort being devoted chiefly to western Canada?
I am told that there is one special pamphlet published by the department and distributed throughout the United States and England dealing with Ontario alone.
But the agents as a rule are devoting their energies to promoting immigration to western Canada.
I am told that Ontario gets about one-third of the total immigration.

I have seen reports stating that about 100,000 settlers were brought into Ontario last year. The department have, I believe, eighty-six agents appointed in Ontario for placing immigrants on their arrival and, according to a return brought down in the House a short time ago, there were only 1,356 placed by these eighty-four agents in Ontario. There is surely something radically wrong in regard to the figures that have been published in the press when
it is stated that these eighty-six agents who have been appointed in Ontario have only been able to place 1,356 people during the last year. There is no use talking, there is something wrong in regard to the methods of bringing out and placing agricultural help in this province. The energies of the department have for years been confined almost entirely to promoting immigration to western Canada. Ontario has, for some reason or other, been singled out by the late Government as the one province where little or nothing would be done, and I am sorry to say that the same system has been continued by the present Government and that no reform has been made in that direction.
To-day, instead of attempting in any way to do justice to that province, they are depending on the provincial Government and not only depending on the provincial Government, but the different counties are organizing and forming associations to bring people into these counties and to see that the requirements are looked after. In view of the enormous expenditure for immigration some reformation should be made in regard to this matter. In my own county last week I noticed that there was a meeting called by the various boards of 'trade and that an association was formed with this object in view. The same thing occurred in Middlesex, Norfolk, Lambton and a great many other counties because of the fact that the system that has been in vogue in this province for the last eight years is considered a joke. They do not think of making application to the Department of the Interior for the help that is required on the farm. Why is not the same policy pursued in regard to Ontario that is pursued in the West? I notice in the report, made to the department by Mr. J. Bruce Walker, Commissioner of Immigration at Winnipeg, that in that city there is an office where they receive applications for farm help from the farmers of western Canada and they endeavour as far as possible to supply the demand there. There is nothing of the kind in existence in Ontario.
The province is being drained of every man who is available every year to meet the requirements of the West. Even before the crops are ready for the harvest large excursions are run from every town and village in Ontario and every inducement is being offered to the labourers of the province to go to western Canada and harvest the crops there. The railways, I believe, are doing something that they should not be permitted to do in that respect. They are giving transportation for about ten dollars from points in Ontario to any point in western Canada, but you can get that rate only at these particular times. In view of the condition of affairs, I think

it is very important and very essential that the department should see that the requirements of the farmers of Ontario are met to some extent at least. You have a great many officials in Ontario, but you have no office where applications for farm help are received. You have eighty-four agents this year, and you had eighty-six last. They are termed agents, but they receive no salary. Their instructions are: that if they will communicate with a booking agent in Great Britain, get people to come out here, and place them on a farm in Ontario, they will get a commission for every one so placed. All the work that is being done and all the money thas is being expended is entirely outside of that. You allow a beggarly commission of two dollars-or it may be five dollars-I am not sure which-
Two dollars.

-for getting into communication with a British booking agent, and placing -a man upon an Ontario farm. Very few agents succeed under this system, and Ontario is being neglected in that respect. You say to the man who is appointed that he will get his little commission of two dollars if he will induce somebody to come out and settle in Ontario. There are a great many counties in Ontario in which not a single man has been placed by any of these agents or by any means of the department during^ the past year. Instead of getting better it is getting worse year after year. There should be some better system adopted in that province, a province that lias contributed generously towards promoting the welfare of Canada, and which does not take any exception to a generous expenditure in this direction. But we do insist that we shall receive fair treatment along with every other province in that respect That is being denied to us to-day. I submit that the system that is in vogue in this Dominion in regard to the province of Ontario is a discriminatory one, that the agents of the maritime provinces and of the province of Quebec are permitted to go to the port of landing,. engage labourers and place them in {hose provinces. Until last year the province of Ontario was denied that privilege. The British booking agent was told that he would not receive the commission or bonus of five dollars each on the immigrants that were sent to Toronto through the instrumentality of the Provincial Government. That has been remedied by the present Government. I go even further than that and say that you should establish in Ontario a system similar to that which they have in western Canada. In Winnipeg, as I have said, they have an office where applications for farm help are received and where an effort is put forth to provide help. I Mr. SUTHERLAND.
have here the report of Mr. J. Bruce Walker, Commissioner of Immigration, and I will read what he says on the matter:
The department, as you are aware, takes no part whatever in finding employment for skilled labour, but foT the unskilled labourer who is anxious for employment at agricultural work, as well as at railway construction, the Labour Bureau of this office arranges immediate employment. During the past year the applications for experienced help received at this office numbered 17,716, while we were able to place only 11,189.
In that office alone 11,189 were placed, whereas in all the broad province of Ontario there were only 1,356 placed by the eighty-six agents of that province. There never was such a dearth of farm labour in Ontario as there is to-day. During the naval debate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) told us there were enough unemployed men in Calgary alone to man a navy, but I can tell him that he will not find any unemployed men in the province of Ontario. It is as difficult to-day to get farm labour in Ontario during the winter months as in any other season of the year. There are thousands of acres of the best land in that province that are to-day practically producing nothing for want of labour. Ontario has been neglected in this respect in the past, and I contend it is absolutely necessary that the Government should see that justice is done to that province in this respect. From year to year we are increasing the vote for this purpose; last year over half a million dollars was exipended in the United States, and it would appear from the supplementary estimates that the Government is about to greatly increase the agencies in Great Britain. But, so far, we have heard of nothing been done to meet the requirements of Ontario. Of course, it is only a short time since the present Government came into power, and there has been in the interval a change in the head of the Department of the Interior. The present minister unfortunately has been ill, and has not been able to devote attention to the matter, and the Interior Department is being administered by the Minister of Labour who has a great deal of work to do in his own department, I believe that if justice is to be done to Ontario it will be necessary to separate the immigration branch from the Department of the Interior. We have had a member from western Canada head of the Interior Department for a great many years past, and it is probably only right and proper that that should be so, but in my opinion the immigration branch shpuld be entirely separated from the Department of the Interior and some one minister should have charge of it who will see that equal justice will be done to every province and the requirements of the different .parts of the Dominion attended to. If that were

the case you would not find the state of affairs referred to by the hon. .member for Red Deer, who told us tha't in Calgary alone there were-, enough unemployed to man a navy.
He was romancing.

He made the statement anyway and we know as a matter of fact that in certain seasons of the year there are a great many men out of employment in the cities of western Canada. We also know, according to the report of Mr. J. Bruce Walker, that they had placed 11,195 immigrants from that office alone, and we know that the whole 86 agents only placed 1,356 men in Ontario. This is a question that demands 'the immediate attention of the Government. I might refer to the fact that in a great many of the very best counties of Ontario not a single man was placed, and in some of these counties the census returns show the population has decreased more rapidly than in others. For example, in Dufferin, Waterloo, Essex and Perth, not a single man has been placed by the Dominion Government; in Elgin ten men were placed; in Huron thirteen; and in Lambton four. Twenty-eight agents did not place any; eight placed one each. The county councils of Lambton, Norfolk and Middlesex have organized themselves and entered on a propaganda in the old country to supply the counties with labour, entirely ignoring the Government immigration service. The fact that these counties have decided to depend on their own resources is an illustration of the injustice done, not only to those counties, but to almost every county in the province of Ontario.

I have listened to the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) with a great deal of interest, and I have to ask him a favour. Last year he put some figures on record showing the falling off in the rural population in many important counties in Ontario. If the hon. member has these figures at hand I will be much obliged ,if he would put them on ' Hansard ' ; they show how the cities are increasing and how the rural population is falling off.

I 'am sorry I have not the figures at hand, but it is easy to find them in the census returns. In the old rural settled districts of Ontario, outside of some of the newer districts, there has been an actual falling off of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 140,000 in the population during the past ten years. I regret to say that practically very little effort is being made by the Government to settle the lands in northern Ontario. We hear .a great deal about western Canada in the literature published and circulated broadcast through Great Britain and the United States, but
we hear nothing of Northern Ontario, and many people do not realize that we have still unsettled there millions and millions of acres of the best land to be found in the world. Some reasonable effort should be made to induce settlers to go on that land. It may 'be said that the federal Government controls the lands in western Canada and that the province of Ontario owns and controls the lands in Ontario, but that is not sufficient justification for the discrimination which takes place. I think the same evenhanded justice should be dealt out to every province. That is another reason why I believe the Immigration Department should be separated entirely from the Department of the Interior.

Following what my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has said, complaining that immigration has gone to the West rather than to Ontario, I find from the homestead returns that there were 10,000 fewer homestead entries made during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1913, than in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1911, so that, if immigration has gone to the West, it has not gone on to the land. I am afraid that the tendency of immigration has been to the towns rather than to the land, either in the West ot in the East. I just bring these figures to the attention of the hon. minister and of the Government for their careful consideration,

and for such action as they may deem necessary in the matter. I further find, by a comparison of figures given by the hon. Minister of Finance in his budget speech that the proportion of immigration coming from continental Europe is increasing _ in comparison with the proportion coming from the British Isles and from the United States. It is desirable that we should as far as possible keep up the proportion coming from the British Isles, however high our flow of immigration reaches.

In the year 1909-1910
there were 59,790 immigrants from the British Isles; 103,000 from the United States and 45,000 from other countries. In the year 1910-1911 there was a very great change; there were 123,000 from the British Isles as against 121,000 from the United States. In the year 1911-1912 there were
138.000	from the British Isles as against
133.000	from the United States. Last year there were 150,000 from the British Isles as against 139,000 from the United States. Therefore the proportion is getting larger.

I was not making that comparison; I was making the comparison between the proportion coming from the British Isles and the proportion coming from continental Europe. The proportion from continental Europe is increasing more rapidly than that from the British Isles.
That seems to be true. In the year 1911-1912, the total from all other countries was 82,000. In the year 1912-1913, the total was 112,000.

When we reach the supplementary estimates, I would like to get some information from the hon. Minister of the Interior as to the number of Canadians who are leaving Canada for the United States. In the province from which I come there is a constant drain of our young people to the United States. I understand a record is kept of all those who go to the United States with the intention of living there, and there is a working agreement between the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada by which this information is obtained from the officers of the United States Government. I am informed that correspondence is taking place between the department and the post offices in various parts of Canada, inquiring the reasons why our young people go across the boundary line for the purpose of remaining there. It would be interesting if that information were tabulated and were available to members of Parliament.
A few days ago I received from a gentleman in my constituency a very interesting letter in which an inquiry was made as to a young man who had left that part of the country to go to the United States with the intention of remaining there permanently.

A letter was sent from the Department of the Interior to the postmaster in the village of Sherbrooke, where this young man lived, asking him to ascertain why this young man had left for the United States. The letter is as follows:
Sir,-It has been brought to my attention that the party, whose name and address is given below, went duriBg the month of August last to the United States with the object of taking up permanent residence there. Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. W. Scott.
The name of the young man is Lloyd Fielding Pye, age seventeen, Canadian, residence, Sherbrooke, N.S.; intended residence, Salem, Mass. This letter was handed to the father of the young man, and he was asked to give the reason why his son had left Canada. This is the letter sent to the department.
Sir,-Your inquiry of 11th instant addressed to the postmaster at Sherbrooke, N.S., has been handed to me for reply. The boy, Lloyd Fielding Pye, aged 17 is my third son, born 'at Sherbrooke, N.S.j as were also his seven brothers and one sister.
The reason he and others have left this part of the country is-the want of transportation facilities. This part of the country has been and is at present producing a good class of citizens, much better than the European immigrants; but the products of our labour cannot reach a market until its value is used up in transport charges, therefore the labourer or producer must go to the market of his labour or production. The Canadian Pacific railway was built into British Columbia when it had less white oopulation than this county, Guysborough. Truly British Columbia has grown but there have been more people left Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and went to the United States, never to return, than the whole population of all that part of Canada, west of Manitoba, leaving the old folks and the little children at home. The former, unable to work the farm, struggle along unproductive, then die; the latter go to join their brothers and sisters in the United States, as soon as their age will allow them to work in a Massachusetts factory, leaving many old abandoned homesteads so overgrown with spruce and fir that now and

for some years past our lumbermen have been cutting and shipping to the United States lumber that grew on the exact spot which formerly grew grain or vegetables.
So long as our country is governed by politicians instead of, statesman who care nothing for our people unless and until they have a vote, we must expect our natural resources to lie undeveloped, and our best crop, our fellow Canadians, to be gathered and harvested by a Government that knows the worth of our Citizens better than our own Government does. In this particular case, a brother preceded him by two years and there are five more brothers may follow as soon as they are old enough, probably one of them this coming summer and with companions as well, for some families here have as many relations in the United States as they have here. Give us railway communication with the markets for what we produce and our boys will stay home, and some of those who have gone will return.
Yours truly,
C. W. Pye.
I hope that letter will soften the already soft heart of the Minister of Railways, though I do not read it for that purpose. It suggests a very interesting phase of the works of the Department of the Interior and I think it would be interesting if we could discover the reason why so many of our young people go to the United States. If this information is in such shape that it could be tabulated to be placed before the members of the House, I am sure it would be read with great interest.

The young men referred to by the hon. member for Guysborough do not need to go to the United States to get employment in factories; they could find splendid employment at remunerative salaries in the province of Ontario and other provinces in manufacturing establishments of the same kind. They must have had some other reason.

I understood the
minister to state that of the 402,000 immigrants that came to Canada last year, 122,798 came to Ontario. If anything were required to condemn the system that has been in vogue for placing farm labourers in Ontario, this statement would do it. Last year 1,356 men were placed by the eighty-six agents in Ontario. We are told of 122,000 people coming, and we know of the thousands of men required on the farms of Ontario. As to these 122,000, we know that, as a matter of fact, a great many of them were returned Canadians, and not immigrants at all. We know also that a great many of those who come into Ontario , or into the other older provinces want to engage only for a short period, and other are diverted from their destinations by agents, their intention being to see the West as soon as possible, and in a short time they go west. And of the young men growing up in Ontario, tens of thousands have gone west. What I strongly object to is the system that has been pursued by our railways. We have been building railways-we shall be asked in a short time to grant large subsidies to a railway to develop our country-and I believe these railways are doing a rank injustice to the farmers of Ontario by seducing away from their province the help that is necessary to work their farms, by giving low rates at certain seasons of the year, a system that would not be tolerated if applied to any other class than those in the rural districts. If you ascertain the ultimate destination of the larger portion of this 122,000, you will find that it is not the province of Ontario. The very fact that we have so large an immigration into Ontario as shown by the figures condemns the system adopted in this province. I may say, candidly, it was adopted in this province for political purposes, to prevent the province of Ontario from meeting the demands of the province_ in 1907, and it, has been carried on ever since that lime. I had hoped and expected that a change of policy would take place when there was a change of Government', and I exceedingly reyreti to see the old system still in vogue and the same injustice done to the province of Ontario as before.

I do not want to do anything to prevent the passage of the minister's estimates, but the hon. member has brought forward a most interesting question. Will he tell me how the Government is to blame if 122,000 immigrants have come to Ontario and then gone on west, and that so large a portion of the natives of Ontario have done the same ? And would the hon. gentleman point out the remedy ? We in the East are interested, as well as the people of Ontario. They tell us that 19,000 immigrants come to the maritime provinces. But unfortunately, [DOT]after ten years you take the census, you find that you have an increase of not more than 19,000. Our people go away, but we do not think that the Government deliberately plans to take them away.

The hon. membeT would have known that I pointed out the remedy if he had followed my argument. I pointed out that under the system in western Canada, applications are received from the farmers for the help they require, and the department at Winnipeg endeavours to see that the requirements are met. But in Ontario we have no such system. We have a large number of appointees, not on salary as they are in the West, but on commission. The Department of Immigration furnishes them with a list of booking agents in Great Britain and elsewhere to communicate with, and tells them that if they will get an immi-

And they do come into Ontario at the rate of over 120,000 a year. Why do they leave ?

If they come to Ontario, why is not the same means provided to place them ? Is it owing to the lack of system that they come here and then take the next train out of the province ? If that is the system, then I think the argument of the hon. gentleman condemns it more strongly than anything else. If 120,000 come here, there ought to be means to meet some of the thousands of applications sent in by the farmers of the province.

This matter was
brought to the attention of the Minister of the Interior some months ago. He gave it his attention at that time, but, I think, did not arrive at any decision. It will have further consideration.

I understand that last
year about 8,000 Chinese came into this country. They pay a head tax of $500, and obtain employment in this country. The purpose of the head tax was to prevent Chinese immigration, but evidently it has not and is not doing so. For a time after the head tax was raised from $100 to $500, it did have the effect of preventing Chinese immigration, but circumstances have changed, and last year there was an immigration as I have said of 8,000 Chinese, all of whom paid the head tax and are now in employment. Is it the intention of the Government to recognize the fact that the head tax of $500 does not prohibit Chinese immigration ? I think I am safe in saying that the immigration of Chinese into Canada last year was larger than it has been in any other year in the history of this country.

The point raised by my hon. friend is rather a wide one. It may be true that Chinese immigration has increased somewhat, but that increase is largely due to the fact that in the western provinces the demand for labour is so great

that the Chinaman coming in there finds ready employment. Of course one Chinaman always brings two or three others, because when he obtains employment at a satisfactory wage he writes home for his friends. I understand that the Chinamen in Vancouver and Victoria have recently raised their tariff of wages, and all this tends to attract Chinese immigration to western Canada. I quite agree with my hon. friend when he says that this is a matter which requires consideration. A few years ago the head tax of $100 prevented Chinese immigration to a greater extent, perhaps, than the tax of $500 does to-day, because conditions have changed, and there is a ready opening for their services. I think this is a matter that will require consideration at the bands of the Government, with a view to seeing that we do not get too great an immigration of Chinese into western provinces.

Of course my hon. friend is aware that Chinese immigration is not what would be called a free immigration. There are Chinese companies organized for the purpose of promoting that immigration, and they are very strong commercial organizations. They enter into an arrangement with the Chinese whereby the head tax is advanced by the company and repaid dn due course. That is a -perfectly legitimate transaction, of course, which can only be carried on when both the financiers who provide the money and the labourers who earn it are Chinese. My hon. friend must be aware that this is not an ordinary immigration by any means. While I do not want to press the Government on the subject, I take this opportunity of bringing to their attention a condition of facts which is measurably startling, and which certainly calls for consideration, and in my humble judgment, for action.

Would you suggest
raising the tax?
It is not my business to suggest, but it seems to me that that would be a reasonable proposition.
Two days ago we received complaints along the line referred to by my hon. friend, and we are taking the matter into consideration.

Will the minister explain how the disposition of this money derived from the importation of Chinamen is made? I understand that the provinces through which the Chinamen enter Canada receive a certain proportion of the money. Naturally nearly all of the Chinamen enter through British Columbia, but many of them scatter throughout Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Do these provinces receive a share of the money derived from the head tax?
I think I am right in saying that the tax is $500 each, and that half of it goes to the Dominion, and the other half to the province through which they enter.

Naturally, nearly all
of them enter through British Columbia, but many of them go mto the prairie provinces. Would it not be fair for the other provinces to derive a share of the benefit, if it can be called a benefit, of that head tax?

The law has not been changed since 1904, but my hon. friend's suggestion is worthy of consideration.

Indians-Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest territories, $544,498.

I understand that
the grazing lease on the Blood Indian reserve expires on the 1st July, this year, and I understand that petitions ha,ve been presented to the Government, asking that the leases be not renewed, but that instead the Government should establish a new method, if they cannot arrange with the Indians to remove their reserve to some other part of the country. The Blood Indian reserve covers about 550 square miles, or 350,000 acres, and is in the most fertile part of southern Alberta. It is very valuable land, and the people there are particularly anxious that it should be opened up to settlement. It has been the practice in the past to give grazing leases practically for the whole reserve. These will expire on the 1st of July, and it is suggested that, instead of renewing them, small tracts of land should be leased to the settlers in that district so that they can go into the raising of cattle, if the Indians refuse to allow the reserve to he opened up for settlement. At present the farmers, with only one-quarter or one-half .section, have not much opportunity to go in for cattle raising. The people are anxious to have mixed farming developed, and the proposition is made that the Government should provide for small leases to the farmers. The Indians are quite favourable to it. I think it would help to encourage mixed farming and to make the reserve more productive to the people of southern Alberta.

I am very glad that
my hon. friend has brought this matter up, I have had it under consideration for some time and I quite agree, with him that there is a very large tract of country that is substantially non-productive. I think something should be done with it. We are considering it very carefully.
Indians-British Columbia, $135,290.
How could they know?

I do not know how they could know, but my hon. friend can very well realize that the government of a province carrying on business according to the svstem we have-even the members of the British Columbia Government-would not dare to take a quarter of a million dollars out of the treasury of the province and pay it to a band of Indians unless they knew as a matter of fact how they were going to get that money back. They could not know how they were going to get that money back unless they had an understanding with the Dominion Government in regard to that transfer. .
Indians, generally, $107,500.

There are some Indians in my constituency and there are two buildings being put up for the teachers. Thereare two schools, one at Eskas-oni, in North Cape Breton, and the other at Nyanza in Victoria. I understand that the Government has very properly agreed to build houses for these teachers, as the Indian reserve has no suitable place for their accommodation. There is a difficulty about the house bought at Nyanza. It was constructed to be heated with a furnace, but no furnace was put in. The teacher had a pretty hard time last winter, there being no furnace and no other means of heating. I would suggest to the minister that a furnace be put in, as the building was built with that intention. I have not seen the house, but I believe it is very nice, and I think a proper thing would be to put in a furnace, or if not a furnace, to see that the building is heated in some other way.

This is a very large item, the subject is a very important one, but I do not think it would be proper at this

moment to bring up any serious discussion or ask for any large amount of information upon it. I think the only thing to do is to pass it, and perhaps revert to it when we come to the supplementaries and when we will have more time than we have now.

I appreciate what my
hon. friend has said. We will be glad to see that he has every opportunity that he may desire when we come to the supplementary estimates.

I do not wish to make
any remarks myself, but I am sure that the Government would be able to place on record the particulars as to what they are doing, and I should think they would be glad of the opportunity.

The public would be very glad to know about the Canadian national parks, and a concrete statement might be made when the supplementary estimates come up. Now that we have finished the main estimates, and as the Minister of Militia is absent, I would like him to be reminded of the promise he made me the other night, and that the dropped item for the drill hall in Renfrew be put in the additional supplementary estimates.
I will remind the Minister of Militia.
Press it on him hard.
